Calibrate an LPPLS signal across a range of noise levels

Source: R/lppls_noise.R
lppls_noise_sweep.Rd

Adds noise to a known LPPLS signal at each of several levels, recalibrates at every level, and collects the estimates into one table. Because the signal is known, the table shows directly how far each estimate drifts from truth as the noise grows, and how the \(t_c\) likelihood intervals widen with it.

Usage

lppls_noise_sweep(
  signal,
  sd_seq,
  noise = stats::rnorm,
  fit_args = list(),
  seed = NULL,
  fb = FALSE
)

Arguments

signal

Numeric vector, the deterministic log-price path to perturb. Typically the output of eval_lppls().

sd_seq

Numeric vector of noise levels. Each entry scales one draw from noise, and contributes one row to the returned table.

noise

Function of one argument n, returning n standardised innovations. Defaults to stats::rnorm. The draw is multiplied by the current entry of sd_seq, so noise should have unit scale for sd_seq to read as a standard deviation.

fit_args

Named list of arguments passed to fit_lppls(). Use mode = "MPL" for the likelihood-interval columns; without it those columns are NA and noise_tc_plot() has nothing to draw.

seed

Optional integer. When supplied, the generator is re-seeded with it before each level, so every level sees the same innovations scaled differently and the comparison across levels is not confounded by the draw. The caller's random number stream is left as it was. When NULL (default) the levels draw independently, from the caller's stream.

fb

Logical, report progress per level (default FALSE).

Value

A data.frame of class "lppls_noise_sweep", one row per entry of sd_seq, with columns:

sd

The noise level.

tc, m, omega, A, B, C1, C2, D

The parameter estimates.

value

The objective at the optimum.

tc_hat_mpl

The modified profile likelihood estimate of \(t_c\), NA unless fit_args asked for mode = "MPL".

LI5l, LI5u, ...

Lower and upper bounds of each likelihood interval, named for its cutoff as a percentage, so a cutoff of 0.05 gives LI5l and LI5u.

Details

The noise is supplied as a function, so the experiment is not limited to Gaussian errors. Any generator of standardised innovations will do, which is how a heavy-tailed or serially dependent alternative is compared against the Gaussian case on the same signal.

See also

noise_param_plot() and noise_tc_plot() to draw the result; fit_lppls() for the calibration itself.

Examples

# a short, coarse sweep; a real one uses more levels and a longer signal
N      <- 400
signal <- eval_lppls(seq_len(N), A = 8, B = -0.025, C1 = 0.0015,
                     C2 = 0.001, tc = N + 1, m = 0.6, omega = 8)
sweep <- lppls_noise_sweep(
  signal, sd_seq = c(0.01, 0.05),
  fit_args = list(fh = 20, hold_out = 20, num_searches = 1, mode = "F2"),
  seed = 3630
)
sweep[, c("sd", "tc", "m", "omega")]
#>     sd  tc         m    omega
#> 1 0.01 400 0.6055168 8.003865
#> 2 0.05 400 0.6151187 8.237078
